newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Semis - PAR inclusion finally confirmed.
newsitem.headline: Australian Semis - PAR inclusion finally confirmed.

text.p: *Semis perk up after the Reserve Bank of Australia said on Tuesday that it was changing commercial bank's prime asset ratio (PAR) requirements to include state government bonds.

Auustralian semi-government bonds perked up on Tuesday after the Reserve Bank of Australia said it was changing commercial bank's prime asset ratio (PAR) requirements to include state government bonds.

Such a move has been rumoured on an off over the past few years and gathered pace in recent weeks since the federal budget projected a further decline in government debt supply in the coming years. This has seen semi spreads narrowing.
"There has been good two-way flows since the announcement. I think the cut to 3.0 percent from 6.0 percent is a bit more of a surprise to the market," said one bond trader.

The RBA also said it was cutting PAR requirements to 3.0 percent. Under the old PAR requirements banks were required to hold an amount equal to six percent of their liabilities in high quality, readily cashable assets, including notes and coins, and federal government securities.

"Given that it wasn't a certainty, confirmation could see semis spreads could come in a little bit more. But I think most of the move has already taken place," said David Bassanese, senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia.

"The effect is not as big as you might have thought if they had kept the PAR requirement at 6.0 percent. But as long as there is some positive PAR requirement, it is a net positive for semis demand," Bassanese added.

Speculation that semis would be included in PAR, along with news that New South Wales was mulling the sale of its power industry, has seen semis spreads narrow sharply in recent weeks, although prior to Tuesday's announcement traders had felt the market had overdone the PAR speculation.
The NSW Treasury Corp 2006 spread to the benchmark 10-year bond brushed 19 basis points at the start of last week, down from 26 points seen in late April, while short-end spreads were around flat.
